text: This is a game-changer perspective! You're absolutely right that the problem is rarely the data itself—it's asking the right questions. The J.C. Penney example is brilliant because it shows how even perfect analytics fail without causal reasoning. Love how you connected Pearl's Ladder to actual decision-making. The Knowledge Acquisition Tool sounds like exactly what's been missing: turning domain expertise into actionable causal models instead of just historical dashboards. Subscribing to see where this goes! 🚀

text: "Right data, wrong question" should be printed on the wall of every strategy meeting room. The number of decisions being made with rung one tools on rung two problems is staggering. Great breakdown.
author: @RahulManoharDurshinapally

text: I think This is a sharp articulation of why so many “data-driven” decisions still fail in practice. The JC Penney example lands because it shows that accuracy at the association level can still produce strategic blindness. The real shift here is philosophical, from observing systems to deliberately shaping them. Without causal thinking, analytics remains descriptive theater, useful but ultimately disconnected from the decisions that actually determine outcomes.
author: @tooCuriousForYou

text: I couldn't agree more with the premise here. Too many organizations rely entirely on descriptive data and end up just guessing when it comes to implementing changes. Living models seem like the perfect bridge between raw data and true decision intelligence.
author: @JazzyZhang-l4g

text: The 'Do-operator' is the most underrated concept in business analytics. Most organizations are running experiments on their live business because they don't have the causal models to run them in simulation. This is the clearest explanation of why more data doesn't equal better decisions.
